newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Warlord sends forces to power struggle near Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Warlord sends forces to power struggle near Kabul.

text.p: A third army has joined a tense power struggle on sun-baked plains north of Kabul that could determine the fate of the Taleban-ruled Afghan capital.

Powerful Uzbek warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum on Thursday sent a dozen tanks and hundreds of troops to frontlines where the Taleban Islamic militia confronts the army of the government it ousted from the Afghan capital three weeks ago.
Afghan-watchers regard Dostum as heading perhaps the most powerful single fighting force in Afghanistan. His troops deployed on the plains without joining the fighting.
Taleban has rejected an ultimatum from the previous government's military chief to quit Kabul or face bloodshed, saying it has enough fighters to defend the city.
But they might not be able to hold it against both Dostum and the forces of ex-defence minister Ahmad Shah Masood, whose spokesman billed Dostum's deployment as a victory.
Taleban has seized three quarters of Afghanistan, but the Masood forces have counter-attacked north of the capital in recent days, recapturing some towns.
The arrival of Dostum forces on Thursday dramatically escalated the war between Taleban and the former government of Burhanuddin Rabbani.
Dostum's troops and armour poured out of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains, even as he and Taleban were still talking peace.

Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told Reuters in Kabul that Taleban was satisfied with Pakistani-brokered talks in Dostum's northern stronghold and that the Uzbek leader had assured them he would not join the battle.

"Deployment and talks are not necessarily inconsistent. Dostum is clearly making himself the key to a deal and his deployment just strengthens the pressure on the Taleban," said one veteran Afghan watcher in Kabul.
"Even if the Uzbeks join the battle, the hope of successful talks is not dead."

But fears mounted in Kabul of yet another battle for a city that bears the massive scars of factional power struggles in the past four years after escaping largely unscathed Afghanistan's previous 13 years of war.
The United States said it would be willing to support an international arms embargo on Afghanistan to end the civil war.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the demilitarisation of Kabul could also help but it was premature to discuss an international peacekeeping force.
All three proposals have been floated this week at the United Nations. Discussions there on a possible Security Council resolution were reported to be continuing behind the scenes.
Burns told a Washington news briefing the United States would be willing to support a U.N. ban on arms sales to Afghanistan.
"Countries are supplying these factions with arms, and they should stop. The countries surrounding Afghanistan ought to end their active involvement in inflaming this fighting," he said.
While some countries have backed an arms embargo at the U.N., others say it would be impossible to enforce.
Burns said another proposal advanced at a U.N. debate on Wednesday to demilitarise Kabul was "an important idea which we think could be useful and positive in the future".
Two Argentine television journalists were beaten and held for a day by Taleban fundamentalists in Kabul before being released on Thursday, their channel and Argentine officials said in Buenos Aires.
War correspondent Natalio Aides and cameraman Walter Moor, both Argentine nationals, were detained by the new rulers of the Afghan capital on Wednesday but 24 hours later through U.N. mediation.

Dostum's ethnic Uzbeks deployed alongside the forces of Masood, who has pushed back Taleban fighters from the Salang, out of the town of Charikar, a 30-minute drive south, and attacked their main air base at Bagram in the past week.
Witnesses said there appeared to have been little movement on the ground by either side during the day. Taleban have poured hundreds of reinforcements and air power into the battle.
Hundreds of people have fled their villages on the plains where the battle is raging, some heading for Kabul, others north.
